youtube.aciklama:
Does a normal audiogram mean the ear is intact? In this lesson we learn about cochlear synaptopathy, the animal studies of Kujawa and Liberman, ABR wave I amplitude, the difficulty of measuring it in humans, the conflicting findings, and what we can do in the clinic.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will examine the current evidence on hidden hearing loss and cochlear synaptopathy.
We will look at Kujawa and Liberman's animal studies, the difficulty of measuring in humans, conflicting findings and what we can do today.
In the lesson on noise-induced hearing loss we briefly defined cochlear synaptopathy; in this lesson we look at the evidence itself.
The main point where sound is passed to the nerve is the ribbon synapse at the base of the inner hair cell.
Many auditory nerve fibers connect to each inner hair cell; each fiber receives input from only one inner hair cell.
Cochlear synaptopathy is the loss of these synapses while the hair cell itself remains in place.
Once the synapse is lost, the fiber stops working and may degenerate over months or years.
Because the outer hair cells stay intact, the audiogram and otoacoustic emissions can be normal.
As we saw in the lesson on auditory nerve coding, fibers are grouped by their spontaneous rates and thresholds.
Fibers with low spontaneous rates and high thresholds help code sound at high levels and in noisy environments.
Animal studies have reported that these high-threshold fibers are the first to be affected by noise.
This is why it has been proposed that synaptopathy may impair understanding speech in noise.
Because the low-threshold fibers that set the threshold are preserved, the audiogram may not change.

cumleler.yazi: In 2009, Kujawa and Liberman exposed mice to an eight to sixteen kilohertz noise at one hundred decibels for two hours.
cumleler.ses: In two thousand nine, Kujawa and Liberman exposed mice to an eight to sixteen kilohertz noise at one hundred decibels for two hours.

cumleler: The animals showed a clear temporary threshold shift.
Thresholds returned to normal in about two weeks, and the outer hair cells remained intact.
Yet in parts of the cochlea, close to half of the inner hair cell synapses were permanently lost.
Months later, spiral ganglion cells in these regions were also shown to decline.
The study drew wide attention because it showed that a seemingly temporary threshold shift can leave permanent nerve damage.
In animals, the best functional marker of synapse loss is wave I amplitude of the auditory brainstem response, or ABR.
Wave I reflects the synchronous response of the auditory nerve; as working fibers decrease, its amplitude shrinks at high stimulus levels.
In the mouse study, the reduction in wave I amplitude matched the synapse loss.
Since the threshold does not change, this finding can only be seen at high stimulus levels, by measuring amplitude.
Clinically, ABR is usually assessed by latency and threshold; amplitude is used less because it varies widely between people.
This point also explains why moving the animal finding to humans is difficult.
Studies in guinea pigs showed that after noise, mainly fibers with low spontaneous rates were lost.
An important question was whether the synaptopathy shown in mice and guinea pigs also occurs in species closer to humans.
A study in monkeys showed synaptopathy, but it required higher noise levels than in mice.
In mice, synapses were reported to decline with aging even without noise, before thresholds worsened.

cumleler.yazi: A 2019 study of human temporal bones also found clear loss of synapses and nerve fibers with age.
cumleler.ses: A twenty nineteen study of human temporal bones also found clear loss of synapses and nerve fibers with age.

cumleler: So there is direct histological evidence in humans for age-related synaptopathy; for noise-induced synaptopathy, it is more indirect.
In humans, synapses can only be counted after death by temporal bone study; there is no direct measure in a living person.
Wave I recorded from the scalp is a small signal and varies greatly even among healthy people of the same age.
A person's lifetime noise exposure is usually estimated by questionnaire, which relies on memory.
People with a normal audiogram may have loss above eight kilohertz, which affects wave I amplitude and confounds the result.
Factors such as sex, head size and electrode placement also change the amplitude.
So today it is not possible to diagnose synaptopathy in humans with a single measurement.
The candidate measure most used in research is ABR wave I amplitude at high stimulus levels.

cumleler.yazi: In electrocochleography, the ratio of the summating potential to the action potential, or SP/AP, has also been proposed as a marker.
cumleler.ses: In electrocochleography, the ratio of the summating potential to the action potential, or S P to A P, has also been proposed as a marker.

cumleler: Extended high-frequency audiometry is being considered as an early sign of noise damage.
The threshold and size of the acoustic reflex are also studied, since they may be affected by nerve fiber loss.
The envelope following response measures how well the nervous system tracks fast changes in sound amplitude.
Behaviorally, tests of understanding speech in noise or in reverberant rooms are used.
However, none of these measures is a validated clinical test on its own.

cumleler.yazi: In 2016, a larger SP/AP ratio was reported in young adults with high noise exposure.
cumleler.ses: In twenty sixteen, a larger S P to A P ratio was reported in young adults with high noise exposure.

cumleler: In the same study, this group had lower word recognition performance under difficult conditions.
Studies of veterans with heavy noise exposure also found smaller wave I amplitudes.
On the other hand, in a large group of young adults with normal audiograms, no link was shown between noise history and electrophysiology.
Many other studies also found no consistent link between noise history and understanding in noise.
Reasons for the conflicting findings include different groups, different exposure measures and different test methods.
The graph on screen is a teaching example of extended high-frequency audiometry.
In this example, thresholds up to eight thousand hertz are within normal limits.
But above ten thousand hertz, thresholds rise clearly.
A standard audiogram does not show this loss, yet the person may report difficulty in noise.
Some researchers see this loss as an early sign of noise or age damage that may coexist with synaptopathy.
So in a person with a normal audiogram but complaints, checking the extended high frequencies can be informative.

cumleler.yazi: The term hidden hearing loss spread with a 2011 study of tinnitus patients with normal audiograms.
cumleler.ses: The term hidden hearing loss spread with a twenty eleven study of tinnitus patients with normal audiograms.

cumleler: In this study, people with tinnitus had smaller wave I amplitudes, while later waves were preserved.
The authors suggested the central auditory system offsets the reduced nerve input by raising its gain, which may contribute to tinnitus.
Difficulty understanding in noise with a normal audiogram is also a common complaint in the clinic.
But this complaint has other causes as well, such as attention, cognitive factors and auditory processing.
So it is not right to attribute every complaint with a normal audiogram to synaptopathy.

sahneler.baslik: *What can we do* in the clinic?
cumleler: When someone with a normal audiogram reports difficulty in noise, the complaint is taken seriously and documented.
A speech-in-noise test makes measurable a difficulty that a word score in quiet does not show.
If possible, extended high frequencies are tested and a detailed noise history is taken.
People exposed to noise receive counseling on hearing protection and safe listening; this advice helps in every case.
Synaptopathy is a research concept today; it is not written in a report as a definite diagnosis.
Treatment research in this area is also at the animal study stage; no proven treatment is promised to the patient.

sahneler.metin: Instead of telling someone with a normal audiogram but trouble in noise 'your hearing is normal', explain the findings and the complaint together.
cumleler: A clinical tip: do not simply tell someone with a normal audiogram who struggles in noise that their hearing is normal.
Explain that the audiogram measures thresholds in quiet and up to eight thousand hertz, and does not show every hearing skill.
Acknowledge that the complaint is real, share the speech-in-noise result and suggest communication strategies.
This way you avoid both needless worry and dismissing the complaint.

maddeler.metin: Clinic: measure, protect, do not overstate

cumleler: Cochlear synaptopathy is the loss of inner hair cell synapses while the hair cells are intact; thresholds can stay normal.

cumleler.yazi: In 2009, Kujawa and Liberman showed in mice that noise causing a temporary threshold shift left permanent synapse loss.
cumleler.ses: In two thousand nine, Kujawa and Liberman showed in mice that noise causing a temporary threshold shift left permanent synapse loss.

cumleler: In humans there is histological evidence of age-related synapse loss; for noise, findings conflict and no validated test exists.
In the clinic, speech in noise and extended high frequencies are measured, protection is advised, and no definite diagnosis is stated.

cumleler: The correct answer is B: by postmortem temporal bone study.
In a living person, measures such as wave I amplitude give only indirect clues, which is why the debate in humans continues.
